articles.title: Welfare overhaul plans put rare focus on improving benefits system for disabled claimants
articles.summary: Timms review tackles some big questions about a flawed system – but leaves other issues in the ‘maybe later’ drawer
body: Stephen Timms would be forgiven for feeling his thunder has been stolen. The minister for social security has spent the last year reviewing personal independence payments (Pip) in light of Keir Starmer’s doomed measures last summer, but last week the Milburn review pitched a set of changes to the key disability benefit to great fanfare.
But when Timms took to the House of Commons to call for a “fundamental overhaul” of Pip on Tuesday, it was clear these were altogether bigger – and notably not explicitly cost-saving – ideas.

Whereas Milburn proposed £3.6bn in cuts to under-25s’ benefits, Timms offered disability campaigners something they have rarely come to expect from benefit changes: a focus not on shrinking the bill but on making the system better for claimants.

That means tackling the inaccuracy of assessments, particularly for those with fluctuating conditions, and “rehumanising” a process that has long been accused of harming disabled people’s mental and physical health.

The government has already accepted two ideas to this end: introducing a fast-track system that will relieve people with the most severe and easily evidenced conditions from going through an interview, and reducing award reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve – something that will incense critics but win cheers from advocates who have campaigned against “pointless” reassessments since the coalition government phased out lifetime awards as part of Pip’s creation in 2013.

Much of the rest of Timms’s review could be filed in what you might call the “maybe later” drawer: several major but slightly vague changes to the Pip assessment and payments process that ministers will now need to decide whether they want to flesh out and implement.

One key idea is a new impact assessment designed to measure the actual costs that come with someone’s health conditions, with an eye on tailoring payments to needs rather than offering a standard weekly amount for everyone.

Few will be able to deny there is a need to fix the system to target support more effectively: one in six working-age claimants now say they have no additional costs relating to their disability, according to the Resolution Foundation.

For others, meanwhile, Pip doesn’t come close to covering their costs: Scope research last year found the shortfall between the average Pip award and average costs was £630 a month. And yet, years of faulty benefit testing mean campaigners will be highly concerned about whether authorities will be able to accurately work out who needs what or whether it will simply lead to reduced eligibility. With the Timms report saying Pip is “not appropriate” for those who do not incur additional costs, that is an increasingly urgent question to resolve.

Equally challenging will be Timms’s other big proposal, to introduce a “service exchange scheme” where a person would be able to choose to swap part of their financial award for a service, such as access to education or referrals into services such as health or social care.

It would in theory follow a similar model to the longrunning Motability scheme, in which some people swap the mobility component of Pip for a leased car, though how it would affect people’s choice within a service, such as hiring their own care staff, is unknown.
Crucially, any swap would be voluntary, putting Timms at direct odds with Milburn who last week said most young people should lose their right to monthly cash.

For a report that involved a mammoth consultation with more than 38,000 people and organisations, the irony is that in many ways the work has just begun. The government will now consider the review’s recommendations alongside Milburn’s and set out a response in the coming weeks, ahead of a white paper in the new year.
Related: ‘The whole process just doesn’t work’: claimants relive the agonies of Pip assessments

Downing Street will be at pains to stress this is not a competition – that both men have many points of agreements – but it will be hard to shake off the awkward position the government finds itself in, with two different sets of recommendations for one benefit.

Labour MPs who scuppered Starmer’s Pip bill last summer are unlikely to repeat the same rebellion with a popular Andy Burnham premiership. But there will be concern on the left of the party about whether Milburn’s controversial “two-tier” plan to cut benefits for young people will be given the green light.

Others will be vigilant about whether some of Timms’s more minor positive proposals – such as improving assessors’ training and introducing a digital “Tell Us Once” approach so people are not asked to provide the same information again – may get lost in all the noise.
Expect more fireworks when ministers have to decide whether any policies they do adopt will apply only to new claimants or the several million current ones too.

That Burnham is already being warned by some that adopting Timms’s ideas could increase the benefits bill, while others say it will mean hundreds of thousands losing their benefits, sums up the dilemma – and insecurity – that will define the coming months.
For a prime minister who entered office promising he would not bring in “crude cuts”, Burnham may now be asked to put his money where his mouth is.

articles.title: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release
articles.summary: Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east
body: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.
Related: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”
Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary: Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged
body: A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza.
Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.
The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly, in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”
The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.
“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.
The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, said he understood the tribunal’s finding might be appealed so he could not discuss the case in detail. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025, however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

articles.title: New stalking offence to scrap need for proof of fear or distress in England and Wales
articles.summary: Victims’ commissioner welcomes strengthening of law but calls for measures to tackle convicted stalkers
body: Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.

Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.
The move has been welcomed by family members of murdered stalking victims and organisations campaigning on behalf of women who have been the target of sustained harassment.

The parents of 24-year-old Alice Ruggles, who was murdered by her obsessed ex-partner in 2016, welcomed the findings and said they were “heartened” by the government’s commitment to clarify and strengthen the law.
Clive Ruggles and Sue Hills said changes would “bring in due protection for stoic victims like Alice”.

The victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the plan was welcome but added that the announcement was “an opportunity missed” because the government had not introduced measures to tackle convicted stalkers.

A review commissioned last year by the government and led by the barrister Richard Wright, who acted for the prosecution in Ruggles’ case, said the offence of stalking “needs to be both uncoupled from harassment and redrawn in its ambition and scope”.

Under two stalking offences introduced in England and Wales in 2012, the underlying offence of harassment must be established and additional factors such as fear or distress proved for it to be considered stalking.

In his review, Wright said that despite good intentions “we have arrived at a position where there are dozens of offences, all with very similar foundations, all tackling similar behaviour, using slightly different terminology, and having an array of different maximum penalties”.

He said: “If we add to that landscape the minefield of protective orders, with so many varieties and initialisms, created and amended in so many different pieces of legislation, the legislative position as a whole across the realm of interpersonal abuse offences is cluttered and confused.”
Alongside pledging to change the law to make stalking a standalone offence, the government has said it will strengthen sentencing so stalkers could face up to 10 years in prison.

In an immediate change, the Home Office said courts could now directly impose stalking protection orders (SPOs) to protect victims by restricting the alleged perpetrators’ behaviour, even if they have not yet been convicted.

A so-called “super-complaint’ from anti-stalking organisations in 2022 set out concerns including how there had been flawed investigations, instances where stalking was not being properly identified, and police officers “minimising or trivialising” such behaviour.

Waxman, who has been the victim of a stalker for 20 years, said the government had “missed a crucial opportunity by failing to address stalking that continues after conviction”. Her office wanted the government to give police powers to arrest convicted stalkers who repeat their criminal behaviour on one occasion.
“A conviction should not be a reset button for a stalker. Victims should not be left trapped in a cycle of abuse because the law fails to recognise continuing patterns of behaviour,” she said.

Emma Lingley-Clark, the interim chief executive of the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, said: “We fully support the government’s commitment to introduce a standalone stalking law, which we hope will reduce confusion and increase the shockingly low conviction rate for stalking, which is currently only 1.2% of stalking incidents recorded by police.”

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, police say
articles.summary: Unclear if ‘hostage-taker’ who was killed may have been a hostage as daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre ends
body: Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8am on Tuesday local time, customers and employees were taken hostage – the president initially said there were 30 hostages, but after the final count, police put the number at about 70.
Many of them could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested.
One man was killed, whom De la Espriella and police described as one of the criminals who had allegedly resisted.

“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” said De la Espriella in a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year.

Local media identified the dead man as Haider Muñetón Zapata, 51, whose wife had spent the day searching for him as one of the hostages. She gave an interview to Blu Radio on Tuesday, saying they lived near the supermarket and that he had gone there to buy buñuelos, a type of fried dough ball, before picking her up to take her to work, but had stopped responding to her WhatsApp messages at 8.12am.

Zapata reportedly had no criminal record. Cartagena’s mayor, Dumek Turbay, told local media that when special forces stormed the supermarket, Zapata had allegedly resisted and attacked one of the officers, prompting police to shoot him dead.
Related: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city

In a video released shortly after the operation, De la Espriella described the police action as “extraordinary”, speaking with a gun tucked into his waistband, as he has done on several other public occasions as part of his populist tough-on-crime rhetoric.

The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.
As the lengthy negotiations continued into the night, police used water cannon to disperse dozens of onlookers who had gathered outside the supermarket.

Cartagena’s mayor said that when police stormed the supermarket, some of the hostage-takers tried to blend in with the hostages by removing their hoods and changing out of their black clothes into civilian clothing.
According to Turbay, police then had to screen the hostages before eventually identifying the four who were arrested.
Supermarket employee Héctor Puello, who was taken hostage, told Caracol Radio that he had started his shift in the store’s bakery about two and a half hours before the gunmen arrived.
“First of all, I felt like I had come back to life because those armed men were mistreating us,” he said.

Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, said that when he realised what was happening, he hid inside a cold-storage room with four other employees. “After four hours, we couldn’t stand the cold any longer and came out,” he said, at which point they were captured and taken hostage.
Commenting on the rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.

In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.

Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

articles.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
articles.summary: Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children
body: The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.
Related: Lululemon apologises after Japanese drum row at Great Wall yoga event

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

articles.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends
articles.summary: From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power
body: Two very different European diplomatic dramas played out almost simultaneously last week. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU-UK summit transfixed London, while barely registering on the continent. On Sunday, Cop31 collapsed after a united EU forcefully vetoed a watered-down climate pact, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home.What do these two events reveal about the EU: how it works, what takes up its bandwidth, how it exercises its clout – and where it’s vulnerable?
If you were a consumer of most British media last Friday morning, you could have been forgiven for thinking Britain was going to rejoin the EU before lunchtime.

Live blogs tracked Andy Burnham’s every step in the Europa building, as he arrived for a summit that Downing Street billed as a landmark “reset” but that was actually aimed at sealing a package of relatively narrow post-Brexit fixes. A Cabinet Office “mythbuster” assured voters the forthcoming deal wouldn’t ban smoky-flavoured crisps. Westminster was plunged into passionate debate over whether a technical three-part trade package was a Brexit betrayal by instalments, or a national reckoning.

Across the Channel, the UK’s domestic psychodrama was, well, no big deal. For Le Monde, the only question that mattered about the EU-UK summit – and the one that remains unanswered – was “what does Britain actually want?” For Germany’s FAZ, a “swift UK return” to the EU was in any case “an illusion”.

It was a fair reflection of where things stand. For Britain, the EU remains its single largest trading partner, and the deals to ease border checks on food, link carbon markets and launch a capped youth experience scheme marked domestic progress – politically and, hopefully, economically.

By Monday, indeed, Burnham was touring a supermarket, touting a victory in the battle against the cost of living. For the EU, however, the UK remains a third country like many others. It has bigger fish to fry than the paperwork mountains involved in the UK exporting cheddar (or importing chorizo).

That doesn’t mean the EU is indifferent to London, just that its priorities lie elsewhere. Westminster obsesses over food checks; Brussels is more interested in the hard-power domains where the UK is a valuable, even indispensable partner.

Both sides have moved to integrate the UK into EU military mobility networks and deepen support for Kyiv. They are looking into closer electricity market integration, and operational intelligence sharing on issues such as smuggling gangs.

Beyond those strategic interests, the EU largely saw Friday’s summit as theatre for Britons: a not-too-demanding EU contribution to the delicate Downing Street balancing act that aims to boost struggling businesses and placate pro-EU voters, without handing too much ammunition to the Conservatives or Nigel Farage.

The European Commission and Council presidents played their parts with aplomb. But the harsh underlying reality was that while London was quick to hail a “done deal”, EU member states let it gently be known that actually, no, a dispute over university tuition fees would have to be resolved first.

And beneath it all lay a barely concealed European frustration: Britain keeps submitting shopping lists of bespoke, sector-by-sector fixes, without ever deciding what long-term relationship it really wants. Thinktanks in Paris (Ifri) and London (Institute for Government) made the point: the UK is trapped in what might be called an “incrementalism loop”.

Europe values the UK as a nuclear-armed neighbour, a North Sea energy partner and a security ally. Beyond that, it is not the main character in Europe’s story. So while London decides whether it wants long-term third-country status, Swiss-style dynamic alignment, or a return to the single market, customs union – or even the EU – Brussels won’t lose much sleep waiting for the answer.

If the UK summit showed the EU more or less on autopilot, the concluding hours of Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, showed it exercising some raw institutional muscle – and, simultaneously, exposing its sharpest internal contradictions.

When Cop31 ended almost 48 hours over deadline – making it the longest UN climate summit in history – the headlines were all about what wasn’t there: no overarching pact, because no mention of fossil fuels.

At the centre of the collapse stood the 27 EU member states. Facing intense pressure to sign a watered-down “Antalya pact”, Brussels held firm alongside the UK and vulnerable island nations, formally objecting and pulling the plug on the centrepiece agreement.

The bloc stayed together thanks to three mechanisms. First, EU climate negotiators had – unlike on foreign policy – a binding mandate agreed by environment ministers in October, locking in red lines to defend the bloc’s 2023 pledge to transition away from fossil fuels.

Second, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, and Ireland’s Darragh O’Brien, representing the bloc’s rotating council presidency, worked in tandem, leaving little room for wedges between the Brussels bureaucrats and national capitals.

Finally, member states shared the same economic self-interest. Having already priced carbon at home and rolled out a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, even conservative EU governments had no wish to let international competitors off the hook.

Look closer, though, and it all gets a bit more conflicted. EU finance ministers had strictly boxed in new funding, leaving the bloc demanding maximum ambition on emissions while offering minimum movement on money. To developing nations, European unity looked less like principled leadership and more like a coordinated refusal to pay its share.

Even more striking was the timing back home. As Brussels was lecturing the world on fossil fuel ambition in Turkey, EU lawmakers were finalising a two-year delay to the bloc’s own flagship methane rules for oil and gas importers – giving in to fierce lobbying from fossil fuel companies and the Trump administration.

For Brussels, speaking with one voice in Antalya proved it absolutely can draw global red lines. But it might have a harder time ensuring the green standards it defends with such principle abroad are not quietly dismantled at home.

articles.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
articles.summary: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station
body: China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.
Related: The tortoise and the hare: will China beat the US in the race back to the moon?
On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.
Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.

“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”
Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.
Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.

In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme. The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.
The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.

While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”

China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.

Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

articles.title: Labour ‘committed’ to ban on conversion practices despite calls for proposed law to be scrapped
articles.summary: Exclusive: Campaigners say new legislation in England and Wales could infringe on free speech, parenting and religious freedom
body: Labour is “committed” to banning conversion practices despite growing calls to amend or scrap the proposed law over fears it could stifle free speech, the equalities minister has said.

Bridget Phillipson said there was “no question as to the principle of the bill” and that “normal parenting will not be affected” by the law, which would ban abuse that aims to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity in England and Wales.

“The principle of this is the right one,” she said. “There’s a reason we put it in our manifesto. We made a choice to publish a draft bill for further discussion and we welcome all feedback but there’s no question as to the principle of the bill, which is that we shouldn’t be treating LGBT people in an abusive way in modern society.”

The draft bill, published in June, proposes that people found guilty of conversion practices face an unlimited fine and up to five years in prison. Courts would also be able to issue conversion practice protection orders before serious harm occurs if an individual is deemed at risk of being subjected to an abusive practice, including being taken abroad.

However, the bill has prompted criticism from religious leaders and the former head of Britain’s rights watchdog, with calls for the legislation to be abandoned. Opponents argue harmful practices are already covered in law, and that the bill could threaten parental and religious rights.
The government and proponents of the bill were dealt a blow last week when Hilary Cass, the paediatrician behind a review into children’s gender services, withdrew her support.

Cass, who sits in the House of Lords and was initially quoted in a government press release announcing the bill, said she could no longer support it without radical changes, which she suggested might not be possible.

“The draft bill is already having a chilling effect on healthcare professionals who fear they may be accused of falling far below professional standards, even when they have conducted appropriate and ethical therapy,” she said, giving evidence to a joint committee of MPs and peers scrutinising the bill.

Phillipson said she was grateful for Cass’s feedback and was taking it seriously, adding: “I know the committee will be reflecting on her evidence to make sure that when we bring forward final legislation, we do it in the right way so that parents and healthcare professionals are able to have open and frank conversations on this topic.”

Kai O’Doherty, from anti-LGBT abuse charity Galop, said opponents of the bill had been “creating scenarios we don’t recognise as being conversion practices, and detracting from the actual victims and survivors who are trying to seek protection so others don’t have to suffer what they had to experience”.

They added: “The harm threshold is very high so the opposition to the bill is disingenuous in presenting it as causing any risk of inadvertently criminalising parents or people in the workplace. There are some ways in which the bill is already weaker than international comparators, so it’s critical it does not get watered down.”

Simon Blake, CEO of Stonewall, said some of the examples being given by opponents were “clearly scaremongering”. “Open conversations and disagreements between parents and children won’t be captured,” he said. “We know that health professionals and counsellors have a job that needs to be done, and need to ask robust questions. What they don’t have is a right to try to change somebody based on a predetermined view about their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

The legislation follows years of failed attempts by successive Conservative governments to introduce a ban. Theresa May first pledged to outlaw conversion practices in 2018, as did Boris Johnson in 2019.

Johnson briefly abandoned the plans in 2022 before reversing course after a backlash, but he proposed excluding transgender people from the ban. Rishi Sunak later promised to bring forward legislation, but this did not happen before the Conservatives left office in 2024.

Helen Joyce, director of advocacy at gender-critical campaign group Sex Matters, said: “We want the bill to be withdrawn, not because we want people to be able to commit abuse with impunity, but because the proponents have not demonstrated a need for it, and it will cause an immense amount of collateral damage.”
Joyce argued that what most people think of as a “conversion practice”, such as violence, confinement, sexual assault and physical and psychological abuse, is already a criminal offence.

She said the previous government had made genuine efforts to introduce a ban but struggled to draft legislation that would protect people from abuse without infringing on established human rights, such as freedom of belief and expression, parental authority and protections for family life.

The Church of England has supported a ban on conversion practices relating to sexual orientation since 2017, but a spokesperson said legislation must not “unintentionally criminalise providing appropriate prayer and pastoral care to those who seek it”.
The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales has called for the bill to be abandoned.

Nathan Stilwell, from Humanists UK, said: “Cass is right that it is important we get these definitions right, and they aren’t used vexatiously and wrongly. But what is missing from Cass’s intervention is the experience of people who’ve gone through these conversion practices.”

articles.title: ‘They wanted me to conform’: people abused over sexuality and gender identity tell their stories
articles.summary: Draft bill will ban conversion practices, despite fears from LGBTQ+ groups over effectiveness and consequences
body: From the age of 16, Shash Appan experienced years of abuse from her parents because of her sexuality and gender identity.

It led to her attempting suicide, and then being sent by her family to stay with her grandparents in India – she was told it was for two weeks, but it ended up being two years. She was isolated, unable to travel alone and denied access to a phone or the internet.

“They wanted me to conform to what they saw as normal or natural – they wanted me to be heterosexual, they wanted me to be cisgender,” she said. “They removed any form of gender expression. They would cut my hair, go through my belongings. I was only able to leave after convincing them to let me go and be homeless – they thought I’d come crawling back but I’ve stayed away since.”

Because of her experience, Appan, 30, knows first-hand the importance of the draft conversion practices bill currently undergoing parliamentary scrutiny. If passed, it would ban abusive practices that aim to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity in England and Wales. Perpetrators could face an unlimited fine and up to five years in prison.

But it is meeting growing opposition from groups who say it could inadvertently criminalise parents or healthcare professionals working with LGBT people, and there are fears the final version of the bill could be watered down or it could be dropped entirely.
Kai O’Doherty from Galop, which runs a helpline for LGBTQ+ people experiencing abuse, said the charity frequently helped victims of conversion practices and it was “not a historical phenomenon”.

One recent case involved a young trans man referred to the charity after being subjected to conversion practices including sexual abuse – such as being forced to listen to graphic and explicit descriptions of queer sex acts against his will – as well as coercive control, name-calling and slurs.
He attempted suicide, before being removed from the UK by his parents and prevented from seeking further help.

Another recent case involved a young lesbian woman who contacted Galop from a culturally conservative religious family who threatened to kill her if she did not become straight, and threatened to rape her.
The government’s 2018 National LGBT Survey found that 7% of LGBTQ+ people have been offered or undergone conversion practices, rising to 13% for trans respondents.
Related: As a lesbian woman, I was subjected to conversion practices. We must protect trans people against this abuse | Jayne Ozanne

Ian Tucker-Bell, 56, underwent conversion practices through his church in the 1980s and 90s, starting when he was a teenager. He said that after telling someone within the church he was gay, he was forced to undergo intense prayer and counselling sessions, which involved asking God to heal him, and he was told he faced “eternal damnation” if he did not change.

“It led to years of real mental turmoil and pretending I was straight,” he said. “It was hideous for my mental health and that’s something I still carry today. These kind of conversion practices damage people – I’m 56 now and still carry the scars.”

Tucker-Bell wrote a play based on his experiences, Locusts, which he has performed in Edinburgh and Brighton and has led him to meet many people who share similar stories, some more recent than his own.
“I’m certain it’s still happening. There are branches of the church that have become more liberal, but then there are branches of the church that have become far, far less liberal,” he said.
He said the bill was urgently needed, and he didn’t believe it would prevent religious freedom of expression – he felt much of the opposition to it was “fearmongering”.

“To me, it seems to be very fair, and very focused on practices that damage, as opposed to just expressions of faith,” he said. “Because if a religious practice is teaching someone they are wrong and need to change fundamentally, then that needs challenging. It’s not just a difference of opinion.”

Appan said she welcomed the broad aims of the bill, but was disappointed with some of the detail. She said there was too much focus on punishment and not enough on stopping conversion practices from happening in the first place.

“The punitive measures don’t make me feel better – I don’t want my parents arrested,” she said. “It feels like the onus is all on the victim to report the abuse, instead of getting agencies to take a proactive approach to spotting the signs of abuse and stamping it out.
“There were adults in my life, teachers and medical staff, who were aware of the abuse and could have intervened.”
She also wanted to see better support for survivors, such as emergency housing to help people escape abuse.

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org
